lead: The Panchangam gives for today the readings for the memory of a bishop or priest, and both speak of those who lead. Hebrews says, “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you,” and, in the same breath, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” In Matthew, Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise slave whom the master finds at work when he arrives. The key words are remember and faithful.

set: These are the closing exhortations of Hebrews, a long sermon by an author the Church does not name; it was early received into the Pauline tradition, though most scholars see a different hand from Paul's. It was written for Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to fall back, and it has shown over twelve chapters that Christ fulfils everything in the worship of the old covenant. Now it turns to the practical life of the community.

The passage moves from the leaders who first preached to the community, to Christ who does not change, to the altar and the sacrifice outside the camp, and finally to the sacrifices of praise and sharing that the Christian offers.
str: vv. 7–9: remember the leaders and imitate their faith; Jesus Christ is the same; do not be carried away by strange teachings.
vv. 10–14: we have an altar; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go out to him; here we have no lasting city.
vv. 15–16: through him let us offer a sacrifice of praise, and do not neglect to do good and to share.
kw: Those who “lead”: the bishops and elders of the community. The writer speaks of leaders who have died (v. 7) and then, in v. 17, of living ones whom the community is to obey.
The place of sacrifice. Hebrews says that we have an altar, and the Church has long understood this of the Eucharist, where the one sacrifice of Christ is made present.
The Greek word for “praise” is of the same family as thanksgiving. It recalls Psalm 50:14 and 116:17, and the Church's own word for the Eucharist, which means thanksgiving.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
The community is to look back at those who first gave them the faith, and to follow the same faith. A Church that forgets its founders has lost its roots.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
The leaders pass away, but Christ remains. Faith rests not on the leaders but on the one whom they preached.
We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.

The Church has understood this altar as the table of the Eucharist, from which the faithful eat, and which fulfils the sacrifices of the old covenant. Some scholars see here the cross itself; the two are not opposed, since the Eucharist makes present the sacrifice of the cross.
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
The Christian is a pilgrim. This is not a rejection of the world; it is a reminder that our true home is with God.
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
The praise of the Church goes to the Father through Christ, in his name. It is the sacrifice of the lips: the prayer and thanksgiving of the Church.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
Praise and love of neighbour belong together. The offering of the lips is joined to the offering of the hands.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is a “sacrifice of praise”, naming Hebrews 13:15 among the many names of the Eucharist (CCC 1330), and that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (CCC 1367). The sacrifices of praise and of sharing that Hebrews describes flow from the Eucharist and are joined to it; they do not replace it. The Church also takes verse 7 as the call to honour the memory of her bishops and priests, which is why today's reading is used for the memory of a bishop or priest.

set: This parable ends the first part of Jesus's last great teaching in Matthew, the discourse on the Mount of Olives (chapters 24–25). Jesus has spoken of the destruction of the temple and the end of the age, and has said that no one knows the day or the hour (24:36). The command to “keep awake” (24:42–44) leads into this parable.
Luke has a similar parable (12:41–48), where Peter asks whom it is for. In Matthew the picture is of a steward put in charge of his master's household, to feed his fellow servants at the right time.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise slave?
vv. 46–47: the faithful one is found at work, and he is put in charge of everything.
vv. 48–51: the one who says “My master is delayed” and abuses his fellow servants is surprised and cast out.
kw: Two qualities together: reliable and sensible. A faithful person keeps his trust, and a wise one knows what to do with it.
The steward's task is to feed others. Authority in the household of God is for nourishing others, not for ruling over them.
The master seems to be late. The test is what the servant does when it seems that nothing is happening.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
Jesus asks a question to which everyone must give an answer by his life. Those who have charge of others, in a family, a parish or the Church, are asked the same.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The blessing is for the one at work when the master comes: not waiting idly but doing what he was given to do.
The danger is the thought that there is time. The wicked servant uses the delay as an excuse to do wrong. Jesus asks his followers to be as faithful in the long wait as in the moment.
ch: The Church reads the parable as a call to watchfulness and to responsible service. The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension the coming of Christ in glory is imminent, even though it is not for us to know the times and seasons (CCC 673), and the Church has often applied the parable especially to bishops and priests, who are put in charge of the household of God to give the faithful their food at the proper time, the word and the sacraments.

rite: Today the Panchangam keeps the memory of Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban and gives the readings for the memory of a bishop or priest. We remember him in prayer, as the Epistle asks: “Remember your leaders.” The Panchangam also remembers St Maria Goretti, a young girl of Italy who died in 1902, aged eleven, after defending her purity against an attack, and who forgave her attacker before she died. The Church honours her as a martyr and as a model of forgiveness.
study: The Epistle says, “Remember your leaders”, and asks us to imitate their faith. Who first taught me the faith, and how can I thank them and pray for them?
The faithful slave is found at work. What has the Master put in my charge, and am I doing it as if he might arrive today?
